A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FEAT and retain matching core methods, experiments and proofs. All 29 pages of v1 and 31 pages of v2, including their appendices, are readable and support comparison across the reorganized material.

before.justification: Table 1 reports original free-energy estimation experiments on Gaussian mixtures, Lennard-Jones systems and alanine dipeptide. Figures 2–3 report training dynamics and lattice-field umbrella-sampling results.

after.justification: Original FEAT experiments are retained, alongside new larger-molecule results, preconditioning comparisons, runtime measurements, robustness tests and transfer experiments.

M1.justification: Section 3.6 introduces one-sided FEAT: a Gaussian reference and one diffusion network replace independently learned transport and score networks, with differences computed from separate absolute free energies. Appendix F.3 specifies DDPM transition kernels for this variant. Appendix E.3 also introduces a transferable model conditioned on target scaling.

E1.justification: V2 adds solvation free-energy evaluation on alanine tetrapeptide and Chignolin, extending the molecular coverage beyond alanine dipeptide. Appendix E.3 adds evaluation on unseen Gaussian-mixture scaling factors, including interpolation and extrapolation. The original principal benchmark systems remain.

E2.justification: V1 compares unpreconditioned Neural TI across seven system configurations in Table 1. V2 retains it only for GMM-40 and LJ-79 and adds preconditioned Neural TI for those configurations in Table 2. Five original Neural TI comparison entries disappear. Target FEP and the MBAR references remain.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce discretization/sample-size sweeps, training and testing on different target scales, and larger-network one-sided evaluation with DDPM kernels. The original hyperparameters remain in v2 Table 8. The stated lattice potential changes from λφ² to λφ⁴ (v1 Equation 163; v2 Equation 161), without establishing that simulations were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 retains the estimator-training curves and umbrella example, while adding Neural TI preconditioning ablations, runtime analysis, sensitivity to discretization steps and sample counts, and transfer tests distinguishing interpolation from extrapolation (Table 2 and Appendix E). These directly investigate practical properties largely untested in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions report Table 1 means and standard deviations across three runs with different seeds. The new transfer experiment uses the same three-run mean/standard-deviation practice. No increased replication, new confidence intervals or significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Shared Table 1 FEAT, Target FEP and reference values are unchanged. New results include preconditioned Neural TI estimates of 0.1±0.2 on GMM-40 and 356.9±1.8 on LJ-79, and one-sided FEAT estimates of 109.91±2.55 on ALA-4 and 320.02±0.70 on Chignolin. Tables 4–7 add runtime, sensitivity and transfer results. Five original Neural TI entries are removed.

T1.justification: The central theorems and proof structures remain. Appendix C.2 revises the relative-MSE expression, restores missing squared expectations in variance formulas, and clarifies independence of the optimization bound from α. V2 also corrects the lattice-potential definition and specifies the one-sided SDEs and DDPM kernels, without adding a new central theorem.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and central conclusion retain the headline claims of consistent minimum-variance estimation, variational bounds and unification of equilibrium and non-equilibrium methods. The introduction still claims superiority over Target FEP and Neural TI. Adding 'promising' in the abstract does not materially change these claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for one-sided transport's advantages, Neural TI's preconditioning accuracy/cost tradeoff, and interpolation versus extrapolation. Section 5 introduces a path-space variance explanation and the need to diagnose unreliable estimates. V1's specific multistate-extension and explicit-solvent limitation paragraphs are removed.

D1.justification: V2 adds a PyTorch implementation link and discloses use of a single 80GB H100. Appendices F.3–F.5 document the one-sided network, training budget, EMA, evaluation sample counts, transition kernels and Neural TI preconditioning formulas. Existing general hyperparameters and sampling instructions are largely retained.

R1.justification: V2 positions one-sided FEAT as an extension of DeepBAR and adds citations to Ding and Zhang, Arbel, Heng, Ho and Karras. Liu et al.'s rectified-flow citation is removed. The broader positioning relative to FEP, BAR, TI and non-equilibrium samplers remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order remain. Algorithm 1 moves to Appendix A; experimental comparisons and limitations are locally rewritten; new method and experimental subsections and a Broader Impact paragraph are added. Author affiliations, venue text and citation formatting also change.

P2.justification: Tables 2–7 add displays for preconditioning, larger molecules, runtime, sensitivity and transfer, substantially expanding the experimental presentation. Table 1 is reorganized, Figures 1–2 are redrawn or relabeled, and v1 Figure 3 becomes separate Figures 3–4 with retained content. Algorithm 1 moves to the appendix.

improvement.justification: V1 evaluates Neural TI without preconditioning despite acknowledging its importance; v2 adds that control and reports near-reference estimates in Table 2. Direct runtime and robustness tests, together with documented one-sided molecular experiments, substantially strengthen comparison fairness, empirical support and reproducibility. Neural TI coverage narrows, and the introduction's broad superiority claim remains insufficiently qualified, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the gains.
